transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2027-05-09 11:00 PT
- Duration: 62 minutes
- Redwood: Alex Martinez (AE), Priya Shah (SE), Jordan Li (CSM)
- SignalPath: Maya Rios (CTO), Evan Clark (Head of SRE), Lina Park (Product Ops), Samir Gupta (Security)

Summary:
Quick sync to review the incident on 2027-05-01 that caused a 45-minute degradation and a p99 SLA breach for SignalPath's production traffic. Focus: technical root cause, mitigations in flight, contractual implications, and next steps for both engineering and legal.

Topics:
- Timeline and root cause hypothesis
- Mitigations applied (circuit breaker, fallback model, manual warm pools)
- Observability gaps and runbook updates
- Dedicated capacity / reserved pool options
- SLA amendment and credits discussion

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Martinez: All right, thanks everyone for hopping on. We're gonna run through the postmortem for the May first degradation. I want to be very transparent about what we saw and what we are doing. Priya, do you want to start with the timeline?

[00:22] Priya Shah: Yeah, sure. So timeline first cut — at 02:11 UTC we started seeing elevated tail latency, p95 to p99 jumping, and by 02:30 some requests hit timeouts at the edge. We correlated those with a spike in KV cache misses and also a storage node GC event. There's some noise in the transcription: what we say as KV "cash" on the recordings, but it's KV cache.

[00:45] Evan Clark: Right and from our side we saw the spike in retries too; a lot of the client-side SDK r e- attempts compounded the load. We mistakenly had a higher retry multiplier, so the load amplifed.

[01:05] Maya Rios: To add, this triggered our SLA monitor and it alerted our ops pager, we had customers complaining to support about slow responses and a couple timed out calls. Lina raised the risk to Exec at 03:05.

[01:25] Alex Martinez: Thanks. Priya, can you walk us through the root cause path you're tracking?

[01:35] Priya Shah: Sure. Primary chain appears to be: a GC pause on a storage process in region-2, which increased latency for model KV lookups; that increased request latency, which caused the request queue to spike on the inference runtime. The runtime's circuit breaker thresholds were tuned for typical load, not this sudden compounding of retries. So we had: storage pause -> KV miss spike -> runtime queueing -> high p99 -> retries -> more queueing. Also found an edge-case in our batching logic where non-idempotent requests were re-enqueued causing some duplication.

[02:10] Evan Clark: Do you think the primary trigger is the GC or the retry amplification?

[02:18] Priya Shah: Both. The GC was the initial event, but the amplification made it worse. If retries had been capped we would have kept within our SLO window.

[02:36] Jordan Li: There was a question from Legal (I was cc'd) about whether this is a single-tenant impact or multi-tenant. Evan, you saw primarily tenant A and B?

[02:48] Evan Clark: Correct, mainly those two high-volume tenants. We gave you the tenant IDs in the escalation ticket, but we'll re-share.

[03:00] Maya Rios: From contract POV, the p99 breach triggers credit calculations. We need a formal incident summary for our procurement/legal team.

[03:12] Alex Martinez: Understood. Jordan will coordinate that.

[03:18] Samir Gupta: Quick security note — we checked auth flows and there was no indication of malicious traffic or exfil. Just to be explicit, nothing looks like an attack.

[03:30] Priya Shah: For mitigations we applied two tracks: immediate operational mitigations and medium-term code fixes. Immediate: we raised the circuit breaker thresholds briefly and throttled retries at the edge to stop amplification. We also brought up a warm reserved pool (manual warm-up) to drain queues. Medium-term: fix for batching duplicate re-enqueue and a guard to prevent non-idempotent requeue.

[04:00] Lina Park: How long did the manual warm pool take to spin up? Our tickets show about 12 minutes.

[04:08] Priya Shah: Around that, yes. We're working on faster autoscaling for warm pools; the warm path currently still has cold steps that take too long.

[04:20] Maya Rios: From our perspective, the 12-minute spin-up is a problem. If we had a pre-warmed capacity option for our tier that would help.

[04:30] Alex Martinez: That's a fair ask. We have Redwood Dedicated and reserved pool options — we can propose a short pilot to reserve a small dedicated capacity for your high-volume tenant IDs. That would eliminate warm-up for those queries.

[04:48] Evan Clark: We'll consider. Is that a contractual change?

[04:52] Jordan Li: We can structure it as an add-on capacity commitment; Jordan (me) will follow up with pricing and contract language. For the immediate credit calculation, once we share the postmortem we can propose a remediation credit — run that through legal.

[05:10] Priya Shah: I want to call out observability gaps: we didn't have an end-to-end tracing tag that correlated the storage GC events to the inference request traces easily. We have recommendation to add a distributed trace annotation and a KV cache miss metric exported with tenant tags.

[05:30] Alex Martinez: Great. Action items: Priya runs the replay and benchmark; we'll run it on a dedicated 8-GPU pool to match your workload. Evan, you'll provide tenant list and logs. Jordan will draft the customer-facing postmortem and coordinate with legal.

[05:46] Maya Rios: Can you also include the exact token/character counts that were impacted? Our billing is partly usage-based and we want to double-check the impacted windows.

[05:56] Alex Martinez: Yes we'll include the request counts and a CSV of impacted request IDs.

[06:04] Samir Gupta: A security question: what data residency concerns are there when you spin up a dedicated pool for us? We are in EMEA and need data to stay in region.

[06:14] Priya Shah: We can provision region-scoped Dedicated pools. It will be in your region's pool, and we do not cross-replicate request payloads outside that region for Private/Dedicated in our setup. We'll confirm in writing.

[06:28] Lina Park: On runbook updates, we need a clear playbook for when GC or storage node events happen: thresholds, who to page, and automatic throttles. Can Redwood propose changes?

[06:38] Priya Shah: Yes, we'll produce a runbook update and an automated throttle proposal. One of the proposals is to cap retries per client at the edge and implement a backoff jitter that is tenant-aware.

[06:52] Evan Clark: Can the backoff be configured per-tenant? We'd like to allow higher priority tenants to have different settings.

[06:58] Priya Shah: We can make the throttle rules tenant-aware, yes. That's part of the Dedicated pilot discussion as well.

[07:08] Alex Martinez: I want to be clear about timelines. Priya, what's realistic for the batching duplicate fix and the tracing addition?

[07:16] Priya Shah: Small code patch for duplicate re-enqueue — we can ship a patch in two weeks, hotfix branch. Tracing annotation and exporting tenant-tagged KV metrics — that's about three weeks for full rollout with canary.

[07:30] Maya Rios: Two to three weeks is OK but we need the benchmark ASAP to validate. Can we get results in 48-72 hours?

[07:36] Priya Shah: We'll prioritize the replay for your dataset and aim for 72 hours. That means the initial artifacts and CSV within three days.

[07:44] Jordan Li: Legal/contract: we will send a proposed SLA amendment that defines reserved capacity options and also an appendix describing the credit calculation we used. That should go out within 4 business days.

[07:56] Alex Martinez: Anything on potential root causes we missed?

[08:00] Evan Clark: One more thought: our SDK had an older retry default; we updated it after the incident but we will need a coordinated deprecation plan.

[08:08] Alex Martinez: Good catch. We'll coordinate a joint deprecation notice and SDK upgrade window.

[08:14] Priya Shah: Also found a micro-optimization: a kernel path in the runtime that, under high queue pressure, had a pathological lock contention. We'll instrument that and include flame graphs in the follow-up.

[08:30] Maya Rios: OK, and please include the flame graphs — those are great for our SRE review.

[08:40] Jordan Li: Quick check — any external vendors or third-party infra mentioned? Competing vendors were in conversation but not involved in incident.

[08:48] Alex Martinez: Right, just internal infra.

[08:52] Maya Rios: For communications, please make the postmortem public-facing summary and an internal technical appendix. We need both for our Exec and SRE teams.

[09:02] Alex Martinez: We'll produce both.

[09:06] Samir Gupta: One more note about audit logs — please include the retention window for request metadata used in the postmortem; we need that for compliance.

[09:16] Priya Shah: We'll include retention details and confirm no sensitive payload was stored beyond policy.

[09:24] Alex Martinez: To recap — immediate: Priya runs replay and shares benchmark; Evan uploads logs and tenant list; Jordan drafts postmortem and SLA amendment language; Alex sends customer-facing summary; Priya and Runtime team ship duplicate re-enqueue hotfix (2 weeks) and tracing + metrics changes (3 weeks).

[09:48] Maya Rios: That captures it. We'll expect the first artifacts in 72 hours.

[09:54] Alex Martinez: Great. Any final questions?

[10:00] Evan Clark: No, thank you — appreciate the transparency.

[10:04] Maya Rios: Thank you.

[10:08] Alex Martinez: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invite for a one-week checkpoint and the artifact links.

[10:12] Jordan Li: Links to artifacts to be shared: (1) postmortem doc - link pending, (2) benchmark CSV - link pending, (3) quick runbook draft - link pending.

[10:24] End of meeting.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional mis-transcriptions ("KV cash" -> KV cache; "r e- attempts" -> retries; speaker faint crosstalk). References: shared ticket #INC-6221, internal benchmark spreadsheet (link withheld), proposed SLA language draft v0.1 (link withheld).
